newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberian warlord says militia force dissolved.
newsitem.headline: Liberian warlord says militia force dissolved.

text.p: Liberian warlord Alhaji Kromah said on Monday he was transforming his ULIMO militia, which fought devastating battles with a rival group this year, into a political party.
"ULIMO is no longer an armed organisation, but a proposed political party," Kromah told a crowd of supporters at his residence in Congotown district of the capital Monrovia.

"The task for which ULIMO was organised in 1991 which was to bring back home our people who were languishing in refugee camps in the sub-region is over, and it is now time to talk politics," Kromah told his applauding supporters.
The party would be called the All Liberian Peoples Coalition Party, he said.

The civil war in Liberia, launched by chief warlord Charles Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL) in 1989, has killed more than 150,000 people and forced over half the 2.6 million population into exile in neighbouring countries. Founded by freed slaves in 1847 Liberia is Africa's oldest republic.
ULIMO (United Liberation Movement of Liberia for Democracy) was formed in neighbouring Sierra Leone from the community of refugees, largely from Kromah's fellow Moslem Mandigo tribe.

Kromah's ULIMO, allied with the NPFL, fought gainst the splinter ULIMO-J militia of Krahn warlord General Roosevelt Johnson last April and May. The warfare derailed a regional accord to end the civil, but West African leaders pressured the warlords to sign a new deal last August.

"ULIMO cannot give any more justifications for continuing to exist as a fighting force," said Kromah, whose guerrillas symbolically handed over some weapons to the ECOMOG African peacekeeping force in September but are still heavily armed.
Ministers from a nine-nation West African committee overseeing the peace process in Liberia met in Monrovia on Monday to assess moves towards full disarmament, officially set to start in 10 days.

ECOMOG commander General Victor Malu told the ministers that the Nigerian-led force now had about 15,000 men. Member states last week pledged 2,200 extra troops to boost the force to close to the 18,000 level Malu says is needed for disarmament of Liberia's 60,000 guerrillas.
